content_payload.front_text: y at end of 2+ syllable word = /iː/

slides.teacher_cue: y has a third sound. At the end of a word with two or more syllables, y makes long /iː/: happy, funny, baby, city, party, story. This connects to what you already know: y at the start of a word = /j/ (yes), y at the end of a one-syllable word = /aɪ/ (my, fly), y at the end of a multi-syllable word = /iː/ (happy, party). Three sounds, one letter — position and syllable count are the guide.
slides.expected_response: Students apply the three y rules and produce /iː/ correctly in multi-syllable words ending in y.
slides.correction_move: Review the three y rules side by side. Sort words: yes (y=/j/), my/fly (y=/aɪ/), happy/party (y=/iː/). Establish the syllable-count rule for the third sound.
slides.observation_note: Watch for /aɪ/ substitution in multi-syllable y words — Korean learners who learned y=/aɪ/ may generalise.

content_payload.correction_routine: funny spells final /iː/ with y; tree spells final /iː/ with ee.

slides.teacher_cue: Play both words. Students choose the word that uses final y for /iː/, not ee.
slides.expected_response: Students identify funny as the final y spelling and reject tree as ee.
slides.correction_move: Write both words and circle the spelling that maps to /iː/ in each.
slides.observation_note: Watch for students who know the sound but not the spelling distinction.

content_payload.correction_routine: baby uses final y for /iː/; see uses ee.

slides.teacher_cue: Play both words. Ask students to choose the word where /iː/ is spelled with final y.
slides.expected_response: Students identify baby as the final y word and reject see as an ee word.
slides.correction_move: Contrast the spellings and restate the multi-syllable y rule.
slides.observation_note: Watch whether students can separate sound identity from spelling choice.
